items.readable_text:
Content:
A repeated integral, also known as an iterated integral, is an integral in which we carry out repeated integration with respect to different variables. An example of a repeated integral is as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y]

Content:
To evaluate this integral, we first integrate with respect to the inner variable [MATH: x,] and then with respect to the outer variable [MATH: y]. We can write this more explicitly as

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{1}ye^{xy}dx]dy.]

Content:
We now carry out the integration. First, we integrate with respect to [MATH: x,] treating [MATH: y] as a constant. This gives

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{1}ye^{xy}dx]dy|= ∫_{0}^{1}[(ye^{xy})/(y)]_{0}^{1}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}[e^{xy}]_{0}^{1}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y} − e^{0}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y} − 1dy.]

Content:
Finally, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y} − 1dy|= [e^{y} − y]_{0}^{1}; = [e − 1] − [1 − 0]; = e − 2.]

Content:
We conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y = e-2.]

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate the repeated integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{2}^{4} \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{x^3}{y^2} \, \textrm{d}x \, \textrm{d}y.]
sections.readable_text: Evaluate the repeated integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{2}^{4} \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{x^3}{y^2} \, \textrm{d}x \, \textrm{d}y.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to [MATH: x], treating [MATH: y] as a constant:

[MATH: ∫_{2}^{4}[∫_{0}^{2}(x^{3})/(y^{2})dx]dy|= ∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})[(x^{4})/(4)]_{0}^{2}dy; = ∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})((2^{4})/(4) − (0^{4})/(4))dy; = ∫_{2}^{4}(4)/(y^{2})dy; = 4∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})dy]

Then, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 4∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})dy|= 4[− (1)/(y)]_{2}^{4}; = 4(− (1)/(4) − (− (1)/(2))); = 4 ⋅ (1)/(4); = 1]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Evaluate the repeated integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{2}^{4} \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{x^3}{y^2} \, \textrm{d}x \, \textrm{d}y.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to [MATH: x], treating [MATH: y] as a constant:

[MATH: ∫_{2}^{4}[∫_{0}^{2}(x^{3})/(y^{2})dx]dy|= ∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})[(x^{4})/(4)]_{0}^{2}dy; = ∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})((2^{4})/(4) − (0^{4})/(4))dy; = ∫_{2}^{4}(4)/(y^{2})dy; = 4∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})dy]

Then, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 4∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})dy|= 4[− (1)/(y)]_{2}^{4}; = 4(− (1)/(4) − (− (1)/(2))); = 4 ⋅ (1)/(4); = 1]

Content:
Consider the surface [MATH: z= f(x,y) = 3-x^2-y^2,] defined over the following rectangle:

Content:
[MATH: R=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

Content:
A sketch of our surface and its domain is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/650439affb556f6e0bfba937fe6c7b34]

Content:
The double integral of [MATH: f(x,y)] over [MATH: R,] denoted

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{R}{ f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A},]

Content:
represents the total signed volume bounded between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the planes [MATH: x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1.]

Content:
It can be shown that the double integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} {{(3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}},]

Content:
can be evaluated using the repeated integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1\int_0^1 (3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} y.]

Content:
Notice that we replace [MATH: \textrm d A] with [MATH: \textrm d x\,\textrm d y] when writing our double integral as a repeated integral.

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac y{x^2} \, \textrm d A], where [MATH: D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:2 \leq x \leq 4,\: 0 \leq y \leq 3\right\}.]
sections.readable_text:
Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac y{x^2} \, \textrm d A], where
[MATH: D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:2 \leq x \leq 4,\: 0 \leq y \leq 3\right\}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

[MATH: ∬_(D)(y)/(x^{2})dA|= ∫_{0}^{3}[∫_{2}^{4}(y)/(x^{2})dx]dy]

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to [MATH: x], treating [MATH: y] as a constant:

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}[∫_{2}^{4}(y)/(x^{2})dx]dy|= ∫_{0}^{3}[− (y)/(x)]_{2}^{4}dy; = ∫_{0}^{3}(− (y)/(4) − (− (y)/(2)))dy; = ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy]

Finally, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy|= [(y^{2})/(8)]_{0}^{3}; = (3^{2})/(8) − (0^{2})/(8); = (9)/(8)]
sections.readable_text:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

[MATH: ∬_(D)(y)/(x^{2})dA|= ∫_{0}^{3}[∫_{2}^{4}(y)/(x^{2})dx]dy]

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}[∫_{2}^{4}(y)/(x^{2})dx]dy|= ∫_{0}^{3}[− (y)/(x)]_{2}^{4}dy; = ∫_{0}^{3}(− (y)/(4) − (− (y)/(2)))dy; = ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy]

Finally, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy|= [(y^{2})/(8)]_{0}^{3}; = (3^{2})/(8) − (0^{2})/(8); = (9)/(8)]

Explanation:

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy|= [(y^{2})/(8)]_{0}^{3}; = (3^{2})/(8) − (0^{2})/(8); = (9)/(8)]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's once again consider the integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{ { (x^2+y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}}]

Content:
over the rectangular domain

Content:
[MATH: D=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

Content:
Similar to definite integrals of single-variable functions, this double integral can be defined as the limit of a Riemann sum, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{n,\,\,m \to \infty } \sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta x_i \Delta y_j} }]

Content:
Notice that in the above summation, we could have instead summed over the [MATH: j]'s first and then the [MATH: i]'s, giving

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{m,\,\,n \to \infty } \sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta y_j \Delta x_i} },]

Content:
and this would result in an iterated integral in the reverse order:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}}
= \int_0^1\int_0^1 f(x,y)\ \mathrm{d} y\, \mathrm{d} x.]

Content:
Regardless of the order in which we carry out the integration, the answer will always be the same!

Content:
Moreover, provided that the region [MATH: D] is rectangular, we can swap the order of integration. This means that if

Content:
[MATH: D=[a,b] \times [c,d] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x \leq b, \: c \leq y \leq d \big\},]

Content:
then

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f(x, y)dxdy; = ∫_{a}^{b}∫_{c}^{d}f(x, y)dydx]

Which of the following equalities are true given that [MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

  1. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}y \, \text{d}x]

  2. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}y\, \text{d}x]

  3. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}x \, \text{d}y]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following equalities are true given that
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

1. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}y \, \text{d}x]
2. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}y\, \text{d}x]
3. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}x \, \text{d}y]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We notice that:

  • the limits for the variable [MATH: x] are from [MATH: {\color{blue}0}] to [MATH: {\color{blue}2}], and

  • the limits for the variable [MATH: y] are from [MATH: {\color{red}0}] to [MATH: {\color{red}1}.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∬_(D)e^{sqrt(xy)}dA|= ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{2}e^{sqrt(xy)}dx]dy.]

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{\color{blue}0}^{\color{blue}{2}} \left[ \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} .]

So, the correct answer is "II and III only".
sections.readable_text:
We notice that:

- the limits for the variable [MATH: x] are from [MATH: {\color{blue}0}] to [MATH: {\color{blue}2}], and
- the limits for the variable [MATH: y] are from [MATH: {\color{red}0}] to [MATH: {\color{red}1}.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∬_(D)e^{sqrt(xy)}dA|= ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{2}e^{sqrt(xy)}dx]dy.]

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A
= \int_{\color{blue}0}^{\color{blue}{2}} \left[ \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} .]

So, the correct answer is "II and III only".

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A repeated integral, also known as an iterated integral, is an integral in which we carry out repeated integration with respect to different variables. An example of a repeated integral is as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y]

Content:
To evaluate this integral, we first integrate with respect to the inner variable [MATH: x,] and then with respect to the outer variable [MATH: y]. We can write this more explicitly as

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{1}ye^{xy}dx]dy.]

Content:
We now carry out the integration. First, we integrate with respect to [MATH: x,] treating [MATH: y] as a constant. This gives

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{1}ye^{xy}dx]dy|= ∫_{0}^{1}[(ye^{xy})/(y)]_{0}^{1}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}[e^{xy}]_{0}^{1}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y} − e^{0}dy; = ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y} − 1dy.]

Content:
Finally, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{1}e^{y} − 1dy|= [e^{y} − y]_{0}^{1}; = [e − 1] − [1 − 0]; = e − 2.]

Content:
We conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \int_0^1\int_0^1 ye^{xy}\,\textrm d x\,\textrm d y = e-2.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating a Repeated Integral

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the repeated integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{2}^{4} \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{x^3}{y^2} \, \textrm{d}x \, \textrm{d}y.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to [MATH: x], treating [MATH: y] as a constant:

[MATH: ∫_{2}^{4}[∫_{0}^{2}(x^{3})/(y^{2})dx]dy|= ∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})[(x^{4})/(4)]_{0}^{2}dy; = ∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})((2^{4})/(4) − (0^{4})/(4))dy; = ∫_{2}^{4}(4)/(y^{2})dy; = 4∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})dy]

Then, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 4∫_{2}^{4}(1)/(y^{2})dy|= 4[− (1)/(y)]_{2}^{4}; = 4(− (1)/(4) − (− (1)/(2))); = 4 ⋅ (1)/(4); = 1]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Double Integrals

Content:
Consider the surface [MATH: z= f(x,y) = 3-x^2-y^2,] defined over the following rectangle:

Content:
[MATH: R=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

Content:
A sketch of our surface and its domain is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/650439affb556f6e0bfba937fe6c7b34]

Content:
The double integral of [MATH: f(x,y)] over [MATH: R,] denoted

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{R}{ f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A},]

Content:
represents the total signed volume bounded between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the planes [MATH: x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1.]

Content:
It can be shown that the double integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} {{(3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}},]

Content:
can be evaluated using the repeated integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_0^1\int_0^1 (3-x^2-y^2) \, \mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} y.]

Content:
Notice that we replace [MATH: \textrm d A] with [MATH: \textrm d x\,\textrm d y] when writing our double integral as a repeated integral.

---

Item 6 — Example: Evaluating a Double Integral Over a Rectangular Domain

Example Prompt:
Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac y{x^2} \, \textrm d A], where
[MATH: D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:2 \leq x \leq 4,\: 0 \leq y \leq 3\right\}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

[MATH: ∬_(D)(y)/(x^{2})dA|= ∫_{0}^{3}[∫_{2}^{4}(y)/(x^{2})dx]dy]

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to [MATH: x], treating [MATH: y] as a constant:

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}[∫_{2}^{4}(y)/(x^{2})dx]dy|= ∫_{0}^{3}[− (y)/(x)]_{2}^{4}dy; = ∫_{0}^{3}(− (y)/(4) − (− (y)/(2)))dy; = ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy]

Finally, we integrate with respect to [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{3}(y)/(4)dy|= [(y^{2})/(8)]_{0}^{3}; = (3^{2})/(8) − (0^{2})/(8); = (9)/(8)]

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Order of Integration for Double Integrals on a Rectangular Domain

Content:
Let's once again consider the integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{ { (x^2+y^2) \, \mathrm{d}A}}]

Content:
over the rectangular domain

Content:
[MATH: D=[0,1] \times [0,1] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.]

Content:
Similar to definite integrals of single-variable functions, this double integral can be defined as the limit of a Riemann sum, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{n,\,\,m \to \infty } \sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta x_i \Delta y_j} }]

Content:
Notice that in the above summation, we could have instead summed over the [MATH: j]'s first and then the [MATH: i]'s, giving

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}} = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{m,\,\,n \to \infty } \sum\limits_{i = 1}^m {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^n {f\big( {x_i^*,y_j^*} \big)\,\Delta y_j \Delta x_i} },]

Content:
and this would result in an iterated integral in the reverse order:

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D}{{f\left( {x,y} \right)\, \mathrm{d}A}}
= \int_0^1\int_0^1 f(x,y)\ \mathrm{d} y\, \mathrm{d} x.]

Content:
Regardless of the order in which we carry out the integration, the answer will always be the same!

Content:
Moreover, provided that the region [MATH: D] is rectangular, we can swap the order of integration. This means that if

Content:
[MATH: D=[a,b] \times [c,d] = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: a \leq x \leq b, \: c \leq y \leq d \big\},]

Content:
then

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∫_{c}^{d}∫_{a}^{b}f(x, y)dxdy; = ∫_{a}^{b}∫_{c}^{d}f(x, y)dydx]

---

Item 10 — Example: Changing the Order of Integration

3. [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{2}e^{\sqrt{xy}}\, \text{d}x \, \text{d}y]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We notice that:

- the limits for the variable [MATH: x] are from [MATH: {\color{blue}0}] to [MATH: {\color{blue}2}], and
- the limits for the variable [MATH: y] are from [MATH: {\color{red}0}] to [MATH: {\color{red}1}.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∬_(D)e^{sqrt(xy)}dA|= ∫_{0}^{1}[∫_{0}^{2}e^{sqrt(xy)}dx]dy.]

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} e^{\sqrt{xy}} \,\text{d}A
= \int_{\color{blue}0}^{\color{blue}{2}} \left[ \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}1} e^{\sqrt{xy}}\,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} .]
